id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:2:6
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: urgent referral 5.2 Safe Communication (cid:127) Ask directly and calmly: 'Are you having thoughts of ending your life?' direct questions do not increase risk.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:3
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Listen without judgment; acknowledge the pain.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:4
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Do NOT leave a high-risk person alone.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:5
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Remove access to means: weapons, medications, sharp objects, ropes.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:6
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Involve family or trusted community members if the person consents.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:7
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Make a safety plan: identify warning signs, coping strategies, and who to contact in crisis.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:8
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Refer to mental health specialist or community support worker.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:9
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: NEVER promise confidentiality about a suicide plan safety must come first.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:10
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: Removing the means (weapons, medications) is one of the most effective single interventions.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:11
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: Do NOT dismiss suicidal statements as 'attention-seeking'.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:12
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: GRIEF & BEREAVEMENT IN CONFLICT (cid:127) Grief is a normal response to loss of family, home, or community.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:13
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Normal grief: waves of sadness; crying; preoccupation with the deceased; may last months to years.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:14
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Complicated grief: persistent, disabling grief lasting > 6 months with significant impairment.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:15
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Cultural and religious mourning practices are important support and facilitate where safe.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:16
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Allow the person to talk about the deceased if they wish do not redirect away from grief.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:17
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Do not say 'I know how you feel' acknowledge that grief is unique.

id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3:18
chunk_id: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline_chunk_3
source: 07_mental_health_shock_guideline
text: (cid:127) Refer if: persistent inability to function; suicidal ideation; prolonged inability to eat or care for self.

text: Sources: DermNet NZ Thermal Burns; WHO Fact Sheet on Burns Friction Burns Friction burns occur when skin is abraded rapidly against a surface, combining both a thermal and mechanical injury.

source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Sources: Wikipedia Burn; StatPearls Burn Evaluation Tar and Bitumen Burns Tar and bitumen burns occur in industrial or road construction settings.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:14
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Tar adheres strongly to skin and, if hot, causes deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:15
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (Emergency management literature; burn care references) (cid:127) Do NOT attempt to peel off adherent tar this will remove the underlying skin and worsen injury.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:16
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Cool with water to solidify the tar and reduce ongoing thermal injury.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:17

source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Tar is removed progressively at dressing changes using mineral oil, petroleum jelly, or lipid-based solvents, which dissolve the tar without damaging the wound.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:18
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Treat underlying burn by depth classification once tar is removed.

text: ESTIMATING BURN SIZE (% TOTAL BODY SURFACE AREA TBSA) [Page 10] The size of a burn is measured as a percentage of the total body surface area (TBSA) affected by partial-thickness or full-thickness burns.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:21
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: First-degree (superficial) burns that are only red and not blistering are NOT included and do not influence fluid resuscitation.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10:22
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_10

text: (MSD Manual; WHO Burn Management) Rule of Nines Adults (WHO Burn Management; DermNet NZ; Wikipedia Parkland Formula): Body Region % TBSA Head and neck 9% Each upper

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:2

source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (MSD Manual; WHO Burn Management) Rule of Nines Adults (WHO Burn Management; DermNet NZ; Wikipedia Parkland Formula): Body Region % TBSA Head and neck 9% Each upper limb (arm) 9% each Anterior trunk (chest + abdomen) 18% Posterior trunk (back) 18% Each lower limb (leg) 18% each Perineum / genitalia 1% Palm of hand (including fingers) Approximately 1% Note: The Rule of Nines is modified for children since their heads and lower extremities represent different proportions.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:3
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: RED FLAGS CRITERIA FOR ESCALATION TO SPECIALIST CARE A burn should be considered severe and requiring urgent referral / escalation if any of the following are present (WHO Burn Management; MSF Clinical Guidelines; MSD Manual; WHO Mass Casualty Burns Standards 2024): Burns involving special areas Face, ears, eyes, hands, feet, perineum/genitalia, or over a major joint.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:6
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Burn size Adult: greater than 15% TBSA.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:7
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Pediatric: greater than 10% TBSA.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:8
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Full-thickness burns Any full-thickness burn requires specialist care and cannot heal without surgery.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:9
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Inhalation injury Dyspnoea, wheezing, soot in nares or mouth, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:10
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Ensure airway is patent; high-flow oxygen.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:11
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Chemical or electrical burns Any chemical or electrical burn treat as high risk regardless of external appearance.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:12
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: White phosphorus burns All WP burns are high-risk due to re-ignition potential, systemic toxicity, and cardiac complications.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:13
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Circumferential burns Burns encircling a limb, neck, or chest risk of compartment syndrome or airway compromise.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:14
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Associated trauma / systemic Shock, hypotension, altered consciousness, or significant associated trauma.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:15
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Vulnerable patient groups Children under 3 years, elderly over 60 years, or patients with significant comorbidities.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:16
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: CORE FIRST AID PROTOCOL (Low-Resource / Conflict Setting) The following sequential steps apply to all thermal burn types in low-resource or conflict settings (WHO Burn Management; WHO Fact Sheet on Burns; MSF Clinical Guidelines): [Page 11] STOP the burning STEP 1 Extinguish flames (roll on ground, blanket, or water).

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:17
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Ensure your own safety first.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:18
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: For WP burns: smother with water or wet cloth to exclude oxygen.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:19
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: COOL the burn STEP 2 Cool running water for approximately 20 minutes for burns < 10% TBSA.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11:20
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_11
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Do NOT apply toothpaste, butter, oil, or home remedies.

source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Do NOT apply toothpaste, butter, oil, or home remedies.

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: In large burns (> 10% TBSA) or cold environments, be cautious of hypothermia especially in children.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:5
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: REMOVE constricting items STEP 3 Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight clothing around burned area early, before swelling.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:6
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: COVER the wound STEP 4 Wrap with a clean cloth or sheet or non-adherent sterile dressing.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:7
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: ASSESS severity and ESCALATE STEP 5 Reassess burn depth, size, and location.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:8
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Apply red flag criteria (Section 9).

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:9
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Transport to nearest appropriate facility.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:10
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: The first 6 hours are critical for severe burns.

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Do NOT apply ice directly.

source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: SIGNS OF BURN WOUND INFECTION Initially, burns are sterile.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:19
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Infection is one of the most frequent and serious complications.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:20
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Monitor all burns for the following (WHO Burn Management; DermNet NZ): Burn Wound Cellulitis: (cid:127) Progressive redness, swelling, and pain in uninjured skin surrounding the wound.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:21
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Usually appears within the first few days.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:22
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes responds to penicillin.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:23
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: Invasive Burn Wound Infection: (cid:127) Rapid spread of bacteria from burn eschar into underlying healthy tissues.

id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12:24
chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Signs: change in wound colour, new drainage, foul or sickly sweet odour.

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Common causative organisms: Pseudomonas and other gram-negative bacteria.

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Life-threatening usually requires combined surgical and antibiotic treatment.

chunk_id: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)_chunk_12
source: burn_classification_guideline_v2 (1)
text: (cid:127) Fever is not a reliable sign of infection cellulitis in surrounding tissue is a better indicator.

text: Airway & Breathing Emergencies THIS DOCUMENT IS FOR EMERGENCY REFERENCE ONLY.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Seek professional medical care as soon as it becomes available.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Content is based on established field medicine protocols and does not replace trained medical personnel.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: [Page 2] How to Use This Guide This guide is written for people with NO medical training who must act in an emergency when no doctor or hospital is available.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Every section follows the same structure: Section What it tells you Overview What the condition is and why it is dangerous Signs & Symptoms How to recognize the condition Immediate Actions What to do in the first minutes step by step Ongoing Care What to keep doing until help arrives What NOT to Do Common mistakes that make things worse When to Move Whether and how to transport the person Reference Source of the protocol ALWAYS ensure your own safety first.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not enter an unsecured area, active fire zone, or building at risk of collapse to help someone.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The Universal First Check Do This For Every Patient 1.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If not, wait or move the person to cover.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Shout their name, tap their shoulder.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Watch chest rise for 10 seconds.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Look for blood soaking clothing rapidly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Then go to the specific condition section below.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Post-Pregnancy Emergencies Source: WHO Guidelines for the Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage and Retained Placenta (2009); Mdecins Sans Frontires (MSF) Obstetrics in Remote Settings; UNHCR Reproductive Health in Refugee Situations.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Postpartum Hemorrhage (Severe Bleeding After Birth) Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It occurs when the mother bleeds heavily after delivering the baby.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Heavy bleeding can kill within 2 hours if not controlled.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_0
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Soaking more than one large cloth or pad per 15 minutes Blood pooling rapidly beneath the mother Mother feels faint, dizzy, or confused Pale, cold, clammy skin Rapid, weak pulse (heart beating very fast but faintly) Uterus (belly

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: bleeding can kill within 2 hours if not controlled.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Soaking more than one large cloth or pad per 15 minutes Blood pooling rapidly beneath the mother Mother feels faint, dizzy, or confused Pale, cold, clammy skin Rapid, weak pulse (heart beating very fast but faintly) Uterus (belly below navel) feels soft and floppy instead of firm IMMEDIATE ACTIONS DO THESE IN ORDER 6.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MASSAGE THE UTERUS: Place one hand flat on the lower belly, just below the navel.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Press down firmly and rub in a circular motion.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The uterus should harden like a ball under your hand within 12 minutes.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is the single most important action.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Continue until it stays firm.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: PUT THE BABY TO BREAST: If the baby is able, place it to the mother's breast to suckle immediately.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Breastfeeding causes the body to release hormones that contract the uterus and reduce bleeding.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do this even while massaging.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: CONTROL EXTERNAL BLEEDING: Pack clean cloths tightly against any visible bleeding wound from delivery tears.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Apply direct firm pressure.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not remove cloths add more on top if soaked.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP HER WARM: Cover the mother with any available cloth or blanket.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: ELEVATE HER LEGS: If she is dizzy or unresponsive, lay her flat and raise her legs above the level of her heart using rolled clothing or bags.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This pushes blood toward vital organs.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT LEAVE HER ALONE: Stay with her and monitor continuously.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If bleeding does not slow within 15 minutes of uterus massage, she is in severe danger.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Begin evacuation to any medical facility immediately while continuing care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: [Page 4] Ongoing Care Continue uterine massage every 510 minutes to ensure the uterus stays firm Encourage oral fluids (water, broth) if she is conscious and not vomiting Track her pulse: press two fingers on the inside of her wrist.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: More than 100 beats per minute is alarming.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: More than 120 is critical.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Keep her calm and reassured fear increases blood loss What NOT to Do Do NOT pull on the umbilical cord to deliver the placenta.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This can cause life- threatening hemorrhage and uterine inversion.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT give the mother alcohol.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT leave the placenta inside without medical help beyond 1 hour post- delivery.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_1
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Eclampsia (Seizures During or After Pregnancy) Eclampsia is a dangerous condition where a pregnant or recently delivered woman has seizures due

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: can cause life- threatening hemorrhage and uterine inversion.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT give the mother alcohol.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT leave the placenta inside without medical help beyond 1 hour post- delivery.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Eclampsia (Seizures During or After Pregnancy) Eclampsia is a dangerous condition where a pregnant or recently delivered woman has seizures due to very high blood pressure.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It can occur up to 6 weeks after delivery.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS & SYMPTOMS Sudden seizure (shaking, convulsions, loss of consciousness) Before the seizure: severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of face/hands She may be unresponsive after the seizure for several minutes Confusion or unusual behavior after a seizure IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 12.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: PROTECT HER FROM INJURY: Clear the area around her of hard objects.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not put anything in her mouth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: POSITION: Turn her gently onto her left side during and after the seizure (recovery position).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This keeps her airway clear and reduces pressure on major blood vessels.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: TIME THE SEIZURE: Note when it starts.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is a medical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: AFTER THE SEIZURE: Keep her on her left side.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Talk to her calmly as she regains consciousness.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: Eclampsia requires urgent hospital care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is a life- threatening condition.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: [Page 5] Do NOT put fingers or objects in her mouth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: You will be bitten and it does not help her.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Newborn Not Breathing at Birth Most babies who do not cry immediately after birth can be resuscitated with basic stimulation.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Reference: WHO Basic Newborn Resuscitation (2012).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS FIRST 60 SECONDS ARE CRITICAL 17.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DRY AND WARM: Immediately wrap the baby in a dry cloth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Rub the back and soles of feet vigorously for 30 seconds.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This stimulates breathing.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: CLEAR THE AIRWAY: Wipe the mouth and nose with a clean cloth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not suction unless you have a bulb syringe.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: POSITION: Lay the baby flat on its back with the head in a neutral position (not tilted back, not chin on chest).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:27
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Place a small roll under the shoulders.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:28
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: CHECK BREATHING: Watch for chest rise.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:29
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If breathing: keep warm, give to mother for skin-to-skin contact.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:30
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If NOT breathing after 30 seconds of stimulation: begin rescue breaths.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:31
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: RESCUE BREATHS: Cover both the baby's mouth AND nose with your mouth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2:32
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_2
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Give 5 small, gentle puffs just enough to see the chest

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If breathing: keep warm, give to mother for skin-to-skin contact.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If NOT breathing after 30 seconds of stimulation: begin rescue breaths.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: RESCUE BREATHS: Cover both the baby's mouth AND nose with your mouth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Give 5 small, gentle puffs just enough to see the chest rise slightly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Then give 1 breath every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Check again for breathing.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: IF NO PULSE: If the baby is not breathing and you cannot feel a heartbeat by pressing 2 fingers on the center of the chest, begin CPR: 3 chest compressions (pressing down about 1.5 cm with 2 fingers on the breastbone) followed by 1 breath.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A baby that is limp and blue but warm still has a chance.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Babies can be resuscitated for several minutes after birth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Newborn Hypothermia (Baby Getting Too Cold) Newborns lose heat extremely rapidly, especially in cold or damp environments.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Hypothermia is a leading preventable cause of newborn death in field conditions.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS THE BABY IS TOO COLD IF: Skin is cold to touch on belly or back Lethargic, not feeding, not crying Blue or purple lips and fingernails [Page 6] Breathing slowly or weakly IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 23.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SKIN-TO-SKIN: Place the baby directly on the mother's bare chest, between her breasts.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Cover both with a blanket.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is called kangaroo care and is the most effective rewarming method available without equipment.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: COVER THE HEAD: The baby loses most heat through the head.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Wrap or cover it immediately.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP ENVIRONMENT WARM: Move away from wind, rain, or cold surfaces.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Use body heat from any available adult if the mother is unable.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: FEED: If baby can suckle, breastfeed immediately.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Feeding provides calories and warmth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: REASSESS: After 30 minutes of skin-to-skin contact, the baby should be warmer, pinker, and more active.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Retained Placenta (Placenta Not Delivered) Source: WHO Guidelines for the Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage and Retained Placenta (2009); MSF Obstetrics in Remote Settings.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: After the baby is born, the placenta (afterbirth) should normally deliver within 30 minutes.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If it does not come out, it is called a retained placenta.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is a leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage and requires urgent care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_3
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Placenta has not delivered 3060 minutes after the baby was born Continued moderate bleeding despite a firm uterus Mother feels continued cramping or fullness in

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If it does not come out, it is called a retained placenta.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is a leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage and requires urgent care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Placenta has not delivered 3060 minutes after the baby was born Continued moderate bleeding despite a firm uterus Mother feels continued cramping or fullness in the lower belly IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 28.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT PULL THE CORD: Never pull, tug, or yank the umbilical cord to try to remove the placenta.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is the most dangerous mistake a bystander can make.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It can cause uterine inversion (see 1F) and massive fatal hemorrhage.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: CONTINUE UTERUS MASSAGE: Keep massaging the lower belly to keep the uterus contracted and minimize bleeding.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: ENCOURAGE BREASTFEEDING: Put the baby to breast.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Natural hormones released during suckling help the uterus contract and may help expel the placenta.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP HER UPRIGHT: If able, help her squat or sit upright gravity may assist.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MONITOR BLEEDING: If bleeding increases significantly, treat as postpartum hemorrhage (see 1A).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE: Retained placenta beyond 60 minutes requires manual removal by a trained provider.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Begin evacuation while continuing care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT attempt to manually remove the placenta without medical training.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT pull the cord under any circumstances.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Uterine Inversion (Uterus Turned Inside Out) Source: ICRC War Surgery; MSF Emergency Obstetric Care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Uterine inversion is a rare but immediately life-threatening emergency, most commonly caused by pulling the umbilical cord too hard.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The uterus partially or completely turns inside out through the vaginal opening.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS RECOGNIZE IMMEDIATELY Sudden massive bleeding immediately after delivery A dark red mass visible at or protruding from the vaginal opening Mother goes into shock almost instantly pale, collapsed, unresponsive Severe pain OR no pain at all (if the mother is already in shock) FIELD ACTIONS 34.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PUSH IT BACK IN: Without training and sterile conditions, attempting to replace the uterus causes further injury and infection.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: COVER WITH CLEAN DAMP CLOTH: Place the cleanest available damp cloth gently over the exposed tissue to protect it from drying out and contamination.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: LAY HER FLAT: Elevate her legs.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: She will be in severe shock.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP WARM: Cover her completely.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: This is a surgical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: She will die without intervention.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is the highest evacuation priority.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4:27
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_4
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Uterine inversion is caused by pulling the umbilical cord.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: LAY HER FLAT: Elevate her legs.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: She will be in severe shock.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP WARM: Cover her completely.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: This is a surgical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: She will die without intervention.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is the highest evacuation priority.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Uterine inversion is caused by pulling the umbilical cord.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is why cord traction must never be performed by untrained persons.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Birth Canal Tears (Vaginal and Perineal Lacerations) Source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2017).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: [Page 8] Tears to the vaginal opening and perineum (area between vagina and anus) are very common after delivery, especially first deliveries.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: They cause continuous bleeding that is separate from uterine bleeding.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Continuous slow or moderate bleeding from below, even when the uterus feels firm and contracted Blood flows steadily rather than in gushes Visible wound or tear around the vaginal opening Mother reports sharp pain in the perineal area IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 39.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: APPLY DIRECT PRESSURE: Place a clean folded cloth firmly against the bleeding area and hold steady pressure.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Ask the mother to squeeze her thighs together if able to help maintain pressure.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: HOLD FOR 10 MINUTES: Do not lift to check maintain continuous pressure for a full 10 minutes.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: IF DEEP TEAR: If the wound is deep and pressure alone does not control it, gently pack clean cloth into the vaginal opening and maintain external pressure on top.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: TREAT FOR BLOOD LOSS: Encourage fluids if conscious.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE: Lacerations need suturing to fully stop bleeding and prevent infection.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Distinguish tear bleeding from uterine bleeding: press on the uterus.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the uterus is firm but bleeding continues, the source is a tear, not the uterus.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Both can occur simultaneously.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Newborn Infection (Neonatal Sepsis) Source: WHO Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children; UNHCR Newborn Health in Humanitarian Settings.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Newborn infection (sepsis) is one of the leading causes of neonatal death worldwide.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It develops in the first hours to days after birth, particularly after delivery in non-sterile conditions.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It can kill within 2448 hours if untreated.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_5
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS WATCH FOR THESE IN FIRST 3 DAYS [Page 9] Baby refuses to feed or feeds very weakly when previously feeding well Fever: baby feels hot to touch on the belly or back (OR is abnormally cold both are danger signs) Weak, high-pitched, or unusual cry or no cry at all Belly looks swollen or hard

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: 3 DAYS [Page 9] Baby refuses to feed or feeds very weakly when previously feeding well Fever: baby feels hot to touch on the belly or back (OR is abnormally cold both are danger signs) Weak, high-pitched, or unusual cry or no cry at all Belly looks swollen or hard Skin turns yellow (jaundice) in first 24 hours abnormal, not normal newborn jaundice Rapid breathing (more than 60 breaths per minute) or grunting sounds Baby is limp, floppy, not moving normally Redness, swelling, or discharge around the umbilical cord stump FIELD CARE 44.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP WARM: Skin-to-skin contact with the mother is the best way to maintain safe temperature.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Septic babies lose heat fast.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: BREASTFEED: Breast milk contains antibodies that fight infection.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the baby is too weak to suck, try expressing milk and giving it by spoon or clean finger.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP THE CORD CLEAN: Do not apply anything to the cord stump except letting it air dry.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the cord is infected (red, smelly, discharging pus), cover loosely with clean dry cloth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT GIVE HERBAL REMEDIES OR LOCAL TREATMENTS to a sick newborn.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Neonatal sepsis requires intravenous antibiotics.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: There is no effective field treatment.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A baby that stops feeding is always a medical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not wait to see if it improves on its own.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Umbilical Cord Problems Source: WHO Basic Newborn Care Guidelines; MSF Neonatal Protocols.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Cord Bleeding After Cutting After the cord is cut and tied, the cut end should stop bleeding quickly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If it continues to bleed, the tie was not tight enough.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: RE-TIE the cord tightly with clean string, cloth strip, or shoelace as close to the baby's belly as possible without crushing the skin.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If you have no tie: pinch the cord end between fingers and hold for 5 minutes.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A small amount of oozing is normal.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Active dripping or flowing is not.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Cord Around the Baby's Neck During Birth (Nuchal Cord) [Page 10] Finding the umbilical cord wrapped around the baby's neck during delivery is common and usually manageable.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: FEEL for the cord around the neck as the baby's head delivers run one finger around the neck.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the cord is LOOSE: gently slip it over the baby's head or over the baby's body as it delivers.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_6
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do this calmly and without pulling.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: common and usually manageable.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: FEEL for the cord around the neck as the baby's head delivers run one finger around the neck.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the cord is LOOSE: gently slip it over the baby's head or over the baby's body as it delivers.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do this calmly and without pulling.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the cord is TIGHT and cannot be slipped free: DO NOT FORCE IT.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Continue with the delivery.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Guide the baby's body out in the normal direction the cord will stretch.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not pull or cut the cord at this stage.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: After full delivery: manage cord bleeding as above.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Never cut a cord that is tightly around the neck before the baby is fully delivered this removes the baby's oxygen supply before it can breathe on its own.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Premature Baby (Born Too Early) Source: WHO Kangaroo Mother Care: A Practical Guide (2003); MSF Neonatal Care in Resource-Limited Settings.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A baby born before 37 weeks of pregnancy is premature.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Premature babies are smaller, have thinner skin, and lose heat many times faster than full-term babies.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Hypothermia is the primary killer of premature infants in field conditions.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: RECOGNIZING A PREMATURE BABY Smaller and lighter than expected Thin, almost transparent or red skin Little body fat ribs may be visible Head appears proportionally larger Less active, weaker cry, weaker sucking reflex May have difficulty breathing rapid breathing, nostrils flaring, skin pulling in at ribs IMMEDIATE ACTIONS WARMTH IS SURVIVAL 56.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DRY IMMEDIATELY: Dry the baby vigorously and discard the wet cloth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do not leave the baby on any wet surface even for a moment.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SKIN-TO-SKIN WITHOUT INTERRUPTION: Place the baby directly on the mother's bare chest in an upright position between her breasts.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Cover both completely head included with warm dry cloth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is called Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) and is the single most effective intervention available without equipment.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP SKIN-TO-SKIN CONTINUOUSLY: Unlike a full-term baby, a premature baby must remain in skin-to-skin contact at all times 24 hours a day until it is larger and stronger.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Even brief removal causes dangerous cooling.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: FEED FREQUENTLY: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the baby cannot latch due to weakness, express milk and give by clean spoon or dropper.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A premature baby that is not fed will deteriorate rapidly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MONITOR BREATHING: Count breaths.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Normal for premature newborn is 4060 per minute.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7:27
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_7
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Over 60 with visible effort

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Attempt breastfeeding every 12 hours.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If the baby cannot latch due to weakness, express milk and give by clean spoon or dropper.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A premature baby that is not fed will deteriorate rapidly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MONITOR BREATHING: Count breaths.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Normal for premature newborn is 4060 per minute.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Over 60 with visible effort is a danger sign.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE: Premature babies under 34 weeks gestation require specialist care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Begin evacuation while maintaining kangaroo care it can continue during transport.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Kangaroo Mother Care is endorsed by WHO as equal to incubator care in stable premature infants.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It requires nothing except warmth and proximity.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Any adult (not just the mother) can provide it if the mother is unable.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Maternal Fever and Infection After Birth (Puerperal Sepsis) Source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2017).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Infection of the uterus or birth canal after delivery (puerperal sepsis) is a leading cause of maternal death.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It typically appears 24 hours to several days after birth.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Fever (body feels hot, especially after the first 24 hours post-delivery) Foul-smelling discharge from the vagina Increasing belly pain and tenderness General weakness, chills, rapid pulse Mother appears increasingly unwell rather than recovering FIELD CARE 62.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Keep her hydrated encourage water and fluids constantly if she is not vomiting.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Keep her warm but do not overheat.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Continue breastfeeding infection does not pass to the baby through breast milk in most cases.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT apply anything inside the vagina.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Puerperal sepsis requires antibiotics.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Without treatment it progresses to septic shock and death within days.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Shrapnel & Shard Injuries Source: Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) Guidelines, Committee on TCCC (2023); International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) War Surgery, Volume 1.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Shrapnel injuries result from fragments metal, glass, bone, or debris entering the body at high velocity.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A single explosion can cause dozens of entry wounds.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The most immediately life- threatening are wounds that cause severe bleeding or penetrate the chest or abdomen.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Assess the Injury Do This First Zone Priority Head / Neck CRITICAL risk of airway loss, major vessel bleeding Chest (front or back) CRITICAL risk of collapsed lung, heart tamponade Abdomen / groin CRITICAL internal bleeding likely Arms and legs HIGH control bleeding first Small embedded fragments in skin LOW do not remove in the field 2B.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_8
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Controlling Life-Threatening Bleeding from Shrapnel IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 67.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Chest (front or back) CRITICAL risk of collapsed lung, heart tamponade Abdomen / groin CRITICAL internal bleeding likely Arms and legs HIGH control bleeding first Small embedded fragments in skin LOW do not remove in the field 2B.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Controlling Life-Threatening Bleeding from Shrapnel IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 67.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EXPOSE: Cut away or remove clothing from around the wound to see it clearly.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DIRECT PRESSURE: Press the cleanest material available (clothing, clean cloth) firmly and directly over the wound.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Use your palm or your fist for deep wounds.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: PACK THE WOUND: If the wound is deep or a hole (not a surface cut), push clean cloth INTO the wound with your finger.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This is called wound packing.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MAINTAIN PRESSURE: Hold firm pressure for a minimum of 10 minutes without lifting.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If blood soaks through, add more material on top do not remove the first layer.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: TOURNIQUET FOR LIMB WOUNDS: If bleeding is from an arm or leg and cannot be controlled with pressure, apply a tourniquet (see tourniquet instructions below).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT REMOVE EMBEDDED OBJECTS: If a large piece of shrapnel, glass, or metal is embedded in the body, do NOT pull it out.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It may be plugging a vessel.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Stabilize it in place by padding around it.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Improvised Tourniquet Limbs Only A tourniquet stops blood flow to a limb.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Use it only when direct pressure fails and the wound is on an arm or leg.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: It will cause pain but saves lives.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Use a strip of cloth at least 4 cm (2 inches) wide a torn shirt sleeve, belt, or scarf.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Wrap it around the limb 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (closer to the body, not below it).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie another knot over the stick.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Twist the stick until bleeding stops.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The person will feel severe pain this is expected.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Secure the stick so it cannot unwind.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Write the time applied on the person's forehead or arm with anything available.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT remove the tourniquet.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Only a medical professional should remove it.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:25
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A tourniquet left on longer than 2 hours increases risk of limb loss.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9:26
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_9
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Evacuation to medical care is urgent.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: the person's forehead or arm with anything available.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Do NOT remove the tourniquet.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Only a medical professional should remove it.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A tourniquet left on longer than 2 hours increases risk of limb loss.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Evacuation to medical care is urgent.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Chest Wound from Shrapnel (Sucking Chest Wound) A wound that penetrates the chest wall allows air to enter the chest cavity, collapsing the lung.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: You may hear a sucking or hissing sound with each breath.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Wound in the chest that makes a sucking or bubbling sound when breathing Breathing becomes increasingly difficult and rapid Lips or fingernails turn blue Victim becomes agitated, then unresponsive IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 80.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SEAL THE WOUND: Place the cleanest material available (plastic bag, plastic wrapper, tape) over the wound.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Tape 3 sides only leave one side open to act as a valve.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: If no tape: hold the seal in place with your hand.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIT THEM UP: Help the person sit upright or lean slightly toward the injured side.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: This helps the good lung work better.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: MONITOR: If the person suddenly gets much worse (extreme breathing difficulty, veins in neck bulging, trachea shifting to one side), carefully lift the seal for 12 seconds to release trapped air, then re-seal.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY: A chest wound requires surgical care.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: [Page 14] Do NOT seal ALL four sides of a chest wound.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: A fully sealed wound can trap air and create a tension pneumothorax which kills faster than the open wound.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:17
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Small Embedded Fragments Field Care Multiple small fragments embedded in skin (common in blast injuries) are not immediately life- threatening.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:18
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: In the field without sterile tools, removal attempts often cause more harm than the fragments themselves.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:19
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT attempt to remove small embedded fragments without proper tools and lighting Rinse the area with clean water if available Cover loosely with any clean material to reduce infection risk Mark the locations with a pen if possible to assist later medical care Priority is always the life threats: bleeding, airway, breathing 2F.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:20
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Eye Penetration by Shrapnel or Shard Source: ICRC War Surgery Volume 1; Kuhn F.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:21
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: et al., Ocular Traumatology, Springer (2008).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:22
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Eye injuries from fragments are extremely common in blast and explosion events.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:23
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Any penetrating object in the eye is a surgical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10:24
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_10
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The instinct to remove it is dangerous and must be suppressed.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:0
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: or Shard Source: ICRC War Surgery Volume 1; Kuhn F.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:1
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: et al., Ocular Traumatology, Springer (2008).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:2
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Eye injuries from fragments are extremely common in blast and explosion events.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:3
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Any penetrating object in the eye is a surgical emergency.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:4
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The instinct to remove it is dangerous and must be suppressed.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:5
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: SIGNS Visible object (fragment, glass, metal) in or on the eye Severe eye pain, or complete absence of pain (which may indicate deep penetration) Sudden loss of vision or blurred vision in the affected eye Eye appears deformed, sunken, or fluid leaking from the eye Blood in the white part of the eye or visible beneath the surface IMMEDIATE ACTIONS 84.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:6
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT REMOVE THE OBJECT: Even a small fragment may be holding eye fluid in place.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:7
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Removal causes immediate loss of eye contents and permanent blindness.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:8
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: DO NOT RUB OR PRESS THE EYE: Any pressure on a penetrated eye can force internal contents out.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:9
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: COVER BOTH EYES: This is critical.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:10
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: The eyes move together if only the injured eye is covered, movement of the uncovered eye will cause the injured eye to move too, [Page 15] worsening damage.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:11
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Cover both eyes with a clean cloth or cup shape (do not press on the eye itself let the covering arch over it without touching).

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:12
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP THE PERSON STILL: Ask them not to move their head.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:13
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Lay them flat if possible.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:14
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: KEEP THEM CALM: Fear and movement worsen outcome.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:15
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: EVACUATE URGENTLY: Eye penetration requires surgical care within hours to preserve vision.

id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11:16
chunk_id: field_emergency_guide_v2_chunk_11
source: field_emergency_guide_v2
text: Covering BOTH eyes is not optional it is medically necessary.
