text: Burns Thermal & Chemical How to Use This Guide This guide is for people with no medical training who must act in an emergency before professional help arrives.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Every section uses the same structure: Section What It Tells You Overview What the condition is and why it is dangerous Signs & Symptoms How to recognise the condition Immediate Actions What to do first step by step, in order Ongoing Care What to keep doing until EMS arrives What NOT to Do Common mistakes that make things worse When to Call EMS/Move Explicit criteria for professional care THE UNIVERSAL FIRST CHECK DO THIS FOR EVERY H EMERGENCY Perform these 5 steps before treating any specific condition.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: They apply to every emergency.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 2] ENSURE SCENE SAFETY 1 Do not approach until the environment is safe.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Check for traffic, fire, unstable structures, electrical hazards, or ongoing threats.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Your safety comes first an injured responder helps no one.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK RESPONSIVENESS 2 Shout the person's name and tap their shoulders firmly.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If no response, they are unresponsive.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Shout for help immediately.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CALL EMS NOW 3 Call 911 (or your local emergency number) immediately or direct a specific bystander: 'YOU call 911 and come back to tell me.' Do not assume someone else has called.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK BREATHING 4 Tilt the head back and look for chest rise for no more than 10 seconds.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Normal breathing proceed to step 5.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: No breathing begin CPR (see Section 2).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CONTROL SEVERE BLEEDING 5 Look rapidly for blood soaking through clothing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Press hard with the cleanest material available.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Then proceed to the specific condition section.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n ALWAYS ensure your own safety first.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_0
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Never enter an unsafe scene to help someone.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: begin CPR (see Section 2).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CONTROL SEVERE BLEEDING 5 Look rapidly for blood soaking through clothing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Press hard with the cleanest material available.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Then proceed to the specific condition section.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n ALWAYS ensure your own safety first.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Never enter an unsafe scene to help someone.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Assess before you act a second casualty slows rescue and costs lives.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 3] 1 CHOKING ADULT & INFANT Choking occurs when a foreign object food, a small toy, or fluid partially or completely blocks the airway.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: A complete blockage stops all air exchange and causes unconsciousness within minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Immediate action prevents brain damage and death.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Choking Conscious Adult or Child (Over 1 Year) Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Sudden inability to speak, cry, or make sound (cid:127) Clutching the throat with one or both hands (universal choking sign) (cid:127) Weak, ineffective, or absent cough (cid:127) High-pitched wheezing or no breathing sounds at all (cid:127) Face turns red, then blue (cyanosis) sign of severe hypoxia (cid:127) Panic, wide eyes, frantic gestures Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ASK: 'Are you choking?' If the person can speak or cough forcefully encourage them to keep coughing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: IF THEY CANNOT SPEAK OR COUGH: Stand behind them.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Lean them slightly forward.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: BACK BLOWS: Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Each blow should be a separate, distinct strike.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ABDOMINAL THRUSTS (HEIMLICH): Place one fist above the navel and below the breastbone.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Grip your fist with your other hand.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Give 5 sharp inward-and-upward thrusts.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ALTERNATE: Repeat 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled, the person can breathe and cough, or they lose consciousness.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: IF UNCONSCIOUS: Lower them carefully to the ground.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Call EMS if not already done.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Each time you open the airway to give a breath, look in the mouth if you see an object, remove it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Special Cases (cid:127) Pregnant or very obese: Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts hands on the center of the chest, not the abdomen.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: (cid:127) If alone and choking: Call 911 first if possible.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Attempt self-abdominal thrusts or thrust your upper abdomen sharply against the back of a chair or hard edge.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1:26
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_1
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Choking Infant (Under 1 Year) Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Sudden silence no cry, no cough (cid:127) No visible chest rise (cid:127) Blue or dusky lips and skin Immediate Actions

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Attempt self-abdominal thrusts or thrust your upper abdomen sharply against the back of a chair or hard edge.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Choking Infant (Under 1 Year) Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Sudden silence no cry, no cough (cid:127) No visible chest rise (cid:127) Blue or dusky lips and skin Immediate Actions [Page 4] 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: POSITION: Hold the infant face-down along your forearm, head lower than chest.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: BACK BLOWS: Deliver 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: FLIP: Turn the infant face-up on your other forearm, still head-lower-than-chest.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHEST THRUSTS: Place 2 fingers on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Give 5 quick downward chest thrusts (NOT abdominal thrusts never perform Heimlich on an infant).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK MOUTH: Look in the mouth.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Remove any visible object with your finger.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not perform blind finger sweeps.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: REPEAT: Alternate 5 back blows / 5 chest thrusts until the object is expelled or the infant loses consciousness.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: IF UNCONSCIOUS: Begin infant CPR (see Section 2).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care If the object is expelled and the person is breathing: keep them calm and seated.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Watch for continued coughing, difficulty swallowing, or voice changes the object may still be partially lodged or airway tissue may be bruised.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year this causes organ injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps you may push the object deeper.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT give water or food after choking until the person is assessed by EMS.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT slap the back of a conscious infant while they are upright always lean them forward and downward first.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: When to Call EMS (cid:127) The object is not expelled after repeated cycles (cid:127) The person loses consciousness at any point (cid:127) Breathing does not return to normal after the object is cleared (cid:127) The victim is an infant always call EMS after an infant choking episode [Page 5] 2 SUDDEN CARDIAC ARREST CPR & AED Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) occurs when the heart stops beating effectively.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Blood and oxygen no longer reach the brain.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Brain damage begins within 4 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Death follows within 10 minutes without intervention.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CPR and early defibrillation (AED) are the only field interventions that save lives.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_2
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Every minute without CPR reduces survival by 710%.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: the heart stops beating effectively.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Blood and oxygen no longer reach the brain.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Brain damage begins within 4 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Death follows within 10 minutes without intervention.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CPR and early defibrillation (AED) are the only field interventions that save lives.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Every minute without CPR reduces survival by 710%.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Sudden collapse person drops without warning (cid:127) Unresponsive no reaction to shouts or shoulder tap (cid:127) No normal breathing absent, gasping ('agonal breathing'), or gurgling (cid:127) No pulse detectable at the wrist or neck (cid:127) Lips, fingernails, or skin turning blue (cyanosis) (cid:127) May have a brief seizure-like shaking at onset Immediate Actions Adult CPR (Over 8 Years) 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CONFIRM UNRESPONSIVENESS: Tap shoulders and shout.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Direct a bystander by name: 'You call 911.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK BREATHING: Look for chest rise for no more than 10 seconds.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Gasping is NOT normal breathing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: POSITION: Lay the person on their back on a hard, flat surface.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: HAND PLACEMENT: Heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Second hand on top, fingers interlaced.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COMPRESS: Push straight down at least 56 cm (22.4 inches).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Allow full chest recoil between compressions.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: RATE: 100120 compressions per minute.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Count aloud: '1 and 2 and 3...' Think of a fast song beat.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: RESCUE BREATHS (if trained and willing): After 30 compressions tilt head back, lift chin, pinch nose, give 1 breath over 1 second just until chest rises.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Give 2 breaths, then resume compressions.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COMPRESSIONS-ONLY CPR: If untrained or unwilling to give breaths give continuous chest compressions at 100120/min without stopping.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: This is effective and recommended.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CONTINUE: Until the AED arrives, EMS takes over, the person starts breathing normally, or you are physically unable to continue.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: AED Automated External Defibrillator AEDs are found in airports, malls, gyms, offices, and schools.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: They provide voice instructions.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: POWER ON: Open the AED and press the power button.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:26
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ATTACH PADS: Place pads exactly as shown on the diagram one below the right collarbone, one on the left side of the chest below the armpit.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:27
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Cut or tear clothing away.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:28
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CLEAR AND ANALYZE: Stop CPR.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3:29
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_3
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ensure no one is touching the person.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ATTACH PADS: Place pads exactly as shown on the diagram one below the right collarbone, one on the left side of the chest below the armpit.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Cut or tear clothing away.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CLEAR AND ANALYZE: Stop CPR.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ensure no one is touching the person.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The AED analyzes the heart rhythm.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DELIVER SHOCK: If a shock is advised shout 'CLEAR,' visually confirm no one is touching the person, then press the shock button.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: RESUME CPR: Immediately after the shock (or if no shock advised), resume CPR for 2 minutes before the AED re-analyzes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: REPEAT: Continue CPR + AED cycles until EMS arrives or the person recovers.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CPR Infant (Under 1 Year) 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: 2 FINGERS: Place the middle and ring finger on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COMPRESS: Push down approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: RATE: 100120 compressions per minute.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: BREATHS: Cover both the baby's mouth AND nose with your mouth.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Give 2 gentle puffs just enough to see the chest rise.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CPR Child (18 Years) (cid:127) Use the heel of ONE hand.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Do not stop CPR until EMS arrives or the person shows clear signs of life (normal breathing, movement, coughing).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If the person revives keep them still, warm, and calm.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not give food or water.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Maintain monitoring until EMS arrives.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT begin CPR on a person who is breathing normally it can cause cardiac problems.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT stop CPR to check for pulse more than once every 2 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT remove AED pads once applied.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT wait for the AED before starting CPR start immediately and use the AED as soon as available.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: When to Call EMS Call EMS immediately for any cardiac arrest.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: EMS must be en route before or during CPR.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 7] 3 SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION ANAPHYLAXIS Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that progresses rapidly to airway closure, circulatory collapse, and death often within minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:26
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Common triggers include foods (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts), insect stings, latex, and medications.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:27
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Epinephrine (adrenaline) is the only effective treatment.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:28
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Antihistamines alone are insufficient and dangerously slow.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:29
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms Symptoms appear within seconds to 30 minutes of exposure.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4:30
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_4
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Look for two or more body systems involved: (cid:127) Skin:

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Common triggers include foods (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts), insect stings, latex, and medications.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Epinephrine (adrenaline) is the only effective treatment.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Antihistamines alone are insufficient and dangerously slow.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms Symptoms appear within seconds to 30 minutes of exposure.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Look for two or more body systems involved: (cid:127) Skin: Hives, flushing, swelling of face, lips, tongue, or throat (cid:127) Airway: Hoarse voice, stridor (high-pitched breathing), difficulty swallowing (cid:127) Breathing: Wheezing, shortness of breath, feeling of chest tightness (cid:127) Circulation: Rapid weak pulse, pale or blue skin, sudden drop in blood pressure, dizziness (cid:127) Gut: Nausea, vomiting, severe cramping especially combined with skin or breathing symptoms (cid:127) Neurological: Sudden anxiety, confusion, loss of consciousness Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CALL EMS IMMEDIATELY: Anaphylaxis is always a 911 emergency even if symptoms seem mild at first.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: IDENTIFY EPINEPHRINE AUTO-INJECTOR: Ask if the person carries an EpiPen, Auvi-Q, or similar device.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Check their bag, belt clip, or pockets.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ADMINISTER EPINEPHRINE: Hold the auto-injector in your dominant hand.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Press the tip firmly against the outer mid-thigh (through clothing is fine).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: POSITION: If breathing is difficult sit them upright.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If pale, dizzy, or faint lay them flat with legs elevated.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If unconscious and breathing recovery position on side.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT LET THEM STAND OR WALK: Standing causes blood to pool in the legs and can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse ('empty ventricle syndrome').

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: SECOND DOSE: If symptoms do not improve or worsen after 515 minutes and a second auto-injector is available, administer it in the opposite thigh.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: BE READY FOR CPR: If breathing stops or no pulse is felt begin CPR immediately (see Section 2).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Stay with the person continuously.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Anaphylaxis can have a biphasic reaction symptoms may return 112 hours after apparent recovery.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: All anaphylaxis cases must be transported to hospital by EMS, even after epinephrine improves symptoms.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT give antihistamines (Benadryl) as a substitute for epinephrine they act too slowly for anaphylaxis.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT allow the person to stand or walk if they appear pale or faint.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT assume the person has recovered because symptoms briefly improve.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT delay epinephrine fear of giving an injection is far less dangerous than delaying it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_5
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 8] 4 BURNS THERMAL & CHEMICAL Burns damage the skin and

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:1

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:2

text: Do NOT delay epinephrine fear of giving an injection is far less dangerous than delaying it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 8] 4 BURNS THERMAL & CHEMICAL Burns damage the skin and underlying tissue through heat, chemicals, electricity, or radiation.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Severity is classified by depth.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Cooling is the only first-aid measure proven to change burn outcomes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Chemical burns require continuous flushing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Incorrect home remedies (butter, toothpaste, ice) dramatically increase infection risk and worsen tissue damage.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Burn Classification Degree Depth Appearance Pain 1st Degree (Minor) Surface only Red, dry, no blisters like a sunburn Painful 2nd Degree Into dermis Blisters, wet-looking, deep red or pale Very painful (Moderate) 3rd Degree (Severe) Full thickness White, brown, or black; leathery; dry May be painless 4A.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Thermal Burns Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: STOP THE BURNING: Remove the person from the heat source.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Remove burning or smoldering clothing unless it is stuck to the skin, in which case cut around it, never pull.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COOL THE BURN: Run cool (not cold, not icy) water over the burn for a full 1020 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Start within 3 hours of injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: This is the single most important intervention.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: REMOVE: Gently remove rings, watches, or tight clothing near the burn before swelling begins.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not remove if stuck to skin.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COVER LOOSELY: After cooling, cover with a clean non-fluffy material cling film (plastic wrap) is ideal.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: A clean plastic bag works for hands.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT BURST BLISTERS: Blisters are a natural protective layer.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Intact blisters reduce infection risk significantly.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: TREAT FOR SHOCK: Large or deep burns cause massive fluid loss.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Lay flat, keep warm if shivering, monitor for shock signs.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Chemical Burns Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PROTECT YOURSELF: Put on gloves or use a plastic bag before handling the patient or their clothing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Chemical burns can burn through your skin too.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:26
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: REMOVE CLOTHING: Remove all contaminated clothing, shoes, and jewellery carefully.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:27
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not allow chemical contact with unaffected skin.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:28
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: FLUSH CONTINUOUSLY: Rinse the affected area with large amounts of cool running water for at least 20 minutes for acids, and 60 minutes or more for alkalis (bleach, lime, cement).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6:29
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_6
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT NEUTRALISE: Do not apply baking soda to acid burns or vinegar to alkali burns.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: the affected area with large amounts of cool running water for at least 20 minutes for acids, and 60 minutes or more for alkalis (bleach, lime, cement).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT NEUTRALISE: Do not apply baking soda to acid burns or vinegar to alkali burns.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Neutralisation reactions generate heat and worsen injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COVER: After flushing, cover loosely with clean dry material.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CALL POISON CONTROL: In addition to EMS, call poison control if the chemical is known they can advise on specific antidotes or extended flushing times.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Face or Inhalation Burns Critical Signs n AIRWAY BURN CRITICAL EMERGENCY Singed eyebrows or nasal hair, hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, or soot around the mouth/nose indicate a possible internal airway burn.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The airway can swell shut within minutes to hours.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT wait for breathing difficulty to worsen.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Keep the burned area elevated if possible.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Keep the person warm burned skin loses heat rapidly.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Offer small sips of water if conscious and no airway injury is suspected.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not remove the covering or re-expose the burn.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT apply butter, oil, toothpaste, egg white, or any home remedy all cause infection and seal in heat.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT use ice or ice-cold water causes vasoconstriction and extends tissue damage.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT remove clothing that is stuck to burned skin cut around it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT use fluffy cotton wool or adhesive bandages directly on burns.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:16:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: When to Call EMS (cid:127) Burns larger than the palm of the person's hand (approximately 1% body surface area) (cid:127) Burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or over a major joint (cid:127) Any 3rd degree burn, or suspected deep burn (cid:127) Any chemical burn to the eyes (cid:127) Suspected inhalation burn or airway involvement (cid:127) Burns in children under 5 or adults over 60 (cid:127) Burn caused by electricity always requires hospital evaluation even if minor-looking [Page 10] 5 SEVERE BLEEDING & DEEP CUTS Severe, uncontrolled bleeding is one of the most preventable causes of death.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: An adult can lose a fatal amount of blood in as little as 23 minutes from a major vessel injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Direct, firm, uninterrupted pressure is the primary life-saving action.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Improvised tourniquets on limbs are effective and appropriate when direct pressure fails.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_7
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Blood soaking rapidly

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: An adult can lose a fatal amount of blood in as little as 23 minutes from a major vessel injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Direct, firm, uninterrupted pressure is the primary life-saving action.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Improvised tourniquets on limbs are effective and appropriate when direct pressure fails.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Blood soaking rapidly through clothing a soaked cloth in under 1 minute is severe (cid:127) Blood spurting with each heartbeat (arterial bleeding the most dangerous type) (cid:127) Signs of shock: pale skin, cold clammy sweat, rapid weak pulse, confusion, thirst (cid:127) Large wound with visible deep tissue, muscle, or bone Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PROTECT YOURSELF: Put on disposable gloves from your first aid kit if immediately available.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: EXPOSE THE WOUND: Cut or remove clothing around the wound to see it clearly and control it effectively.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: APPLY DIRECT PRESSURE: Place the cleanest available material (sterile gauze pad, clean cloth) directly over the wound.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Press as hard as you can with your palm or both hands.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PACK DEEP WOUNDS: If the wound is a deep hole or cavity push clean gauze or cloth firmly into the wound with your fingers.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: This is called wound packing.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: HOLD PRESSURE: Maintain continuous firm pressure for a minimum of 10 full minutes without lifting to check.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If blood soaks through add more material on top.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT remove the first layer.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: TOURNIQUET FOR LIMB WOUNDS: If bleeding from an arm or leg cannot be controlled with pressure after 23 minutes apply a tourniquet (see below).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ELEVATE: If the wound is on a limb and no fracture is suspected raise it above the level of the heart to slow blood flow.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: KEEP THEM CALM AND WARM: Fear increases heart rate and blood loss.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Improvised Tourniquet Limbs Only Use when direct pressure fails on an arm or leg wound.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Apply without hesitation when needed.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: MATERIAL: Use a strip of cloth at least 4 cm (2 inches) wide a torn shirt sleeve, belt, or scarf.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Never use wire, rope, or narrow cord they cut tissue.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PLACEMENT: Wrap 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (toward the body, not below).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_8
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: TIGHTEN: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie a second knot over it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Never use wire, rope, or narrow cord they cut tissue.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PLACEMENT: Wrap 58 cm (23 inches) ABOVE the wound (toward the body, not below).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: TIGHTEN: Tie a half-knot, place a stick or pen on the knot, tie a second knot over it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Twist the stick until bleeding stops.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The person will feel severe pain this is expected and normal.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: SECURE: Tie the stick in place so it cannot unwind.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: RECORD TIME: Write the time of application on the person's forehead or arm with a pen, marker, or anything available.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Tell EMS when it was applied.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT REMOVE: Only trained medical personnel should remove a tourniquet.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Embedded Objects [Page 11] (cid:127) If an object (knife, glass, debris) is embedded in the wound DO NOT remove it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: It may be stemming blood flow.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Pad around it to stabilise it in place without pressing on it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Monitor pulse every few minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs of worsening shock (pale, cold, confused) require EMS urgently.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Keep the person lying flat with legs elevated unless injury prevents it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT remove a blood-soaked dressing this disrupts the clot forming underneath.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT use a tourniquet on the neck, chest, abdomen, or groin limbs only.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT remove an embedded object.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT apply a tourniquet using wire, rope, or thin cord they cause tissue damage without stopping bleeding.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: When to Call EMS (cid:127) Bleeding cannot be controlled with 10 minutes of direct pressure (cid:127) Spurting arterial bleeding (cid:127) Deep wounds with visible tissue, tendon, muscle, or bone (cid:127) Any signs of shock develop (cid:127) Wound is on the head, neck, chest, abdomen, or groin [Page 12] 6 SUSPECTED FRACTURES & SPRAINS A fracture is a break in a bone.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: A sprain is a tear or stretch of ligaments around a joint.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Without imaging, it is often impossible to distinguish between them in the field.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Treat any suspected fracture as confirmed.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Open fractures (bone visible) carry serious infection risk and require urgent medical attention.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Mishandling a fracture especially of the spine can cause permanent paralysis.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_9
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Both fracture and sprain: Pain, swelling, bruising at the injury site (cid:127) Fracture-specific: Deformity limb looks bent, shortened, or out of position (cid:127) Grinding or grating sensation when moved (do not test deliberately) (cid:127) Complete inability or

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: fracture especially of the spine can cause permanent paralysis.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Both fracture and sprain: Pain, swelling, bruising at the injury site (cid:127) Fracture-specific: Deformity limb looks bent, shortened, or out of position (cid:127) Grinding or grating sensation when moved (do not test deliberately) (cid:127) Complete inability or strong refusal to use or bear weight on the limb (cid:127) Bone visibly protruding through the skin (open/compound fracture) (cid:127) Numbness or tingling below the injury (nerve involvement) Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: STOP ALL MOVEMENT: Tell the person to stay still.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not try to straighten the limb.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CONTROL BLEEDING: If there is an open wound apply gentle direct pressure around (not on) the wound.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not push exposed bone back in.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: SPLINT IN PLACE: Immobilise the limb in the position you find it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Use any rigid material alongside it a folded newspaper, rolled clothing, or sticks.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Tie above AND below the fracture site not over it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: PAD THE SPLINT: Add soft padding between the rigid splint and the limb for comfort.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK CIRCULATION: After splinting feel that fingers or toes below the fracture are warm.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Can the person feel you touching them?

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If cold, pale, or numb the splint is too tight.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ELEVATE: If possible, rest the injured limb elevated above heart level to reduce swelling.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: COVER OPEN FRACTURES: If bone is visible, cover loosely with a clean, damp cloth.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not attempt to push bone back.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: This is a high infection risk.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: ICE (if available): Apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes to reduce swelling.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Never apply ice directly to skin.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Suspected Spinal Injury CRITICAL CAUTION n DO NOT MOVE A PERSON WITH A SUSPECTED SPINAL INJURY.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Suspect spinal injury after: high-speed accident, fall from height, diving injury, or any trauma with neck pain, back pain, or tingling/numbness in limbs.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Keep the head and neck perfectly still.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not allow the person to sit up.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Only move if the scene becomes life-threatening and you have no other option.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:24
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If you must move them keep the head, neck, and spine aligned in a straight line at all times.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:25
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Keep the person still and warm.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:26
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Re-check circulation distal to the splint every 10 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:27
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not give food or water if surgery may be needed.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10:28
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_10
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Reassure and monitor for signs of shock.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: head, neck, and spine aligned in a straight line at all times.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:1
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Keep the person still and warm.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:2
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Re-check circulation distal to the splint every 10 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not give food or water if surgery may be needed.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Reassure and monitor for signs of shock.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 13] n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT attempt to realign, straighten, or 'reset' a fractured limb.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT apply ice directly to skin wrap it first.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT move a person with suspected spinal injury unless their life is in immediate danger.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT ignore circulation checks after splinting impaired circulation can cause permanent damage.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: When to Call EMS (cid:127) Any suspected fracture of the spine, pelvis, or femur (thigh bone) these are EMS emergencies (cid:127) Open fracture bone visible (cid:127) Circulation below the fracture is impaired (cold, pale, numb) after splinting (cid:127) Signs of shock are present (cid:127) The person cannot bear weight at all after a lower limb injury [Page 14] 7 SEIZURES A seizure is a sudden, uncontrolled electrical disturbance in the brain that causes changes in behaviour, movement, consciousness, or sensation.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Most seizures in people with epilepsy end on their own within 13 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The primary role of a bystander is to protect the person from injury and monitor the situation.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Attempting to restrain a seizure or put anything in the mouth causes more harm than the seizure itself.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:13:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Signs & Symptoms (cid:127) Convulsive (Tonic-Clonic/Grand Mal): Sudden loss of consciousness, body stiffens (tonic phase), followed by rhythmic jerking of limbs (clonic phase) (cid:127) Before the seizure: Some people have a 'warning' (aura) strange smell, vision changes, dj vu, or sudden fear (cid:127) Biting of the tongue or inside cheek (do NOT put anything in mouth to prevent this) (cid:127) Loss of bladder or bowel control (cid:127) Confusion, disorientation, or drowsiness after the seizure ends (post-ictal state) normal, lasts minutes to an hour (cid:127) Absence/Focal seizures: Brief staring spells, subtle repetitive movements (lip-smacking, hand-rubbing), altered awareness Immediate Actions 1.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: TIME THE SEIZURE: Note when it starts.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: This is critical information for EMS.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes is a medical emergency (status epilepticus).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CLEAR THE AREA: Move hard, sharp, or hot objects away from the person.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If they are near stairs or a road protect them, but do not force them to move.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_11
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CUSHION THE HEAD: Place something soft under their head (folded jacket,

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:0
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: minutes is a medical emergency (status epilepticus).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:1

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:2

source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If they are near stairs or a road protect them, but do not force them to move.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:3
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CUSHION THE HEAD: Place something soft under their head (folded jacket, bag).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:4
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Turn them gently onto their side if possible this keeps the airway clear and allows fluids to drain.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:5
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT RESTRAIN: Never hold the person down or try to stop the movements.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:6
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The movements cannot be stopped.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:7
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: DO NOT PUT ANYTHING IN THE MOUTH: The tongue cannot be swallowed.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:8
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Putting fingers or objects in the mouth causes broken teeth, broken fingers, and airway injury.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:9
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: STAY WITH THEM: Monitor breathing throughout.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:10
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: AFTER THE SEIZURE: Turn them onto their side (recovery position).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:11
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: They will be confused and frightened.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:12
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: CHECK BREATHING: Most people breathe normally after a seizure.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:13
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If not open the airway and begin rescue breaths (see Section 2 / Section 5A).

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:14
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Ongoing Care Remain with the person until they are fully conscious and aware.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:15
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: The post-ictal period (confusion after a seizure) is normal and can last up to 3060 minutes.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:16
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do not offer food, water, or medication until fully alert.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:17
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: If they have a medical bracelet or emergency information card read it.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:18
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: [Page 15] n WHAT NOT TO DO Do NOT restrain the person or try to stop the movements.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:19
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT put fingers, a spoon, a wallet, or any object in their mouth.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:20
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT give water, food, or medication during or immediately after the seizure.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:21
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT leave them unattended during or in the immediate aftermath.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:22
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide
text: Do NOT assume recovery monitor breathing closely in the post-ictal phase.

id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12:23
chunk_id: First_Aid_Guide_chunk_12
source: First_Aid_Guide

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Infectious diseases would likely become rampant, and it will be a challenge to maintain sanitary conditions.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Simple activities of daily survival, such as [Page 7] chopping wood, commonly lead to cuts that could get infected.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

text: LONG-TERM SURVIVAL MEDICINE What is wilderness (also referred to as outdoor) medicine?

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:6
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: We define it as medical care rendered in a situation where modern care, training, and facilities are not readily available.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:7
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Wilderness medicine would involve medical care rendered during wilderness hikes, maritime expeditions, and sojourns in less-developed countries.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:8
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: The basic assumption is that trained doctors and modern hospitals exist but are unavailable at the time that medical care is required (perhaps for a significant period of time).

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:9
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: You, as temporary caregiver, will be responsible for stabilizing the patient.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:10
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: That means not allowing the injury or illness to get worse.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:11
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Your primary goal will be the evacuation of the patient to modern medical facilities, even though they might be hundreds of miles away from the location of the patient.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:12
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Once you have transferred your patient to the next highest medical resource, your responsibility to the sick or injured individual will be over.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:13
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Emergency medical technicians (EMTs) or military corpsmen will recognize this strategy as stabilize and transport.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Wilderness medicine Although principles of wilderness medicine have saved many lives, this approach is different from what we would call long-term survival or collapse medicine.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:15
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: In a societal collapse, there is no access to modern medical care and no potential for such access in the foreseeable future.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:16
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: As a result of this turn of events, you would go from being a temporary first- aid provider to being the caregiver at the end of the line.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9:17
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_9
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: You become the highest medical resource left, regardless of whether you have a medical diploma.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Long-term survival medicine Medical training and education for nonphysicians can include wilderness medical classes, EMT, and even military medical corps training.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:7
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: These courses presuppose that you are rendering care in the hope of later transporting your patient to a working clinic, emergency room, or field hospital.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:8
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: If you can make the commitment, this training is very useful to have; its much more likely that youll experience a short-term deficit of medical assistance than a long-term one.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:9
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Despite this, you must plan for the possibility that you will be completely on your own one day.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:10
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: The way you think about this must be modified to fit a day when intensive care units and emergency rooms are inaccessible.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:11
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: You wont have the luxury of passing the sick or injured individual to a formally trained provider, so you must be ready to be there for your patient from start to finish.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:12
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: You will also have to understand how to treat certain chronic medical conditions.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:13
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Even a paramedic, for example, is unlikely to know how to deal with an abscessed tooth or a thyroid condition in the absence of drugs and high technology that may not be available.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:14
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Therefore, you must learn methods that will work in a power-down scenario; you may even have to reach back to older strategies that modern medicine might consider obsolete.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:15
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Using a combination of prevention, improvisation, and prudent use of supplies, you should be able to treat the great majority of problems you will face in a power-down scenario.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10:16
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_10
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Although all of this might seem daunting, we hope to impart enough information in this guide to make you confident in your new role.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: It wouldnt be unusual to see the following: Trauma Minor musculoskeletal injuries (sprains and strains) Minor trauma (cuts, scrapes) Major traumatic injury (fractures, occasional knife or gunshot wounds) Burn injuries (all degrees) Infections Respiratory infections (pneumonia, bronchitis, influenza, common colds) Diarrheal disease (sometimes in epidemic proportions) Infected wounds Minor infections (urinary infections, pinkeye) Sexually transmitted diseases Lice, ticks, mosquitoes, and the diseases they carry [Page 15] Allergic reactions Minor (for example, bites or stings from insects) Major (anaphylactic shock) Dental Toothaches Broken or knocked-out teeth Loss of fillings Loose crowns or other dental work Womens issues Pregnancy Miscarriage Birth control Pregnancy is relatively safe these days, but there was a time in the not too distant past where the announcement of a pregnancy was met as much with concern as joy.

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Sterile technique involves hand washing with special solutions and the use of sterile instruments, towels, and dressings.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:4
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: When used on a patient, the area immediately around these items is referred to as a sterile field.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:5
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: The sterile field is closely guarded to prevent contact with [Page 17] anything that could enable microorganisms to invade it.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:6
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: To guarantee the elimination of all organisms, an autoclavea type of pressure cookeris used for instruments, towels, and other items that could come in contact with the patient.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:7
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: All hospitals, clinics, and medical offices clean their equipment with this device.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Having a pressure cooker as part of your supplies will enable your instruments to approach the level of sterility required for minor surgical procedures.

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Of course, it may be very difficult to achieve a sterile field if you are in an austere environment.

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: To maintain a clean area, certain disinfectants are used.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:14
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Disinfectants are chemical substances that are applied to nonliving objects to destroy microbes.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:15
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: This would include surfaces where you would treat patients or prepare food.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:16
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Disinfection does not necessarily kill all bugs and, as such, is not as effective as sterilization.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:17
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: An example of a disinfectant would be bleach.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:18
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Disinfection removes bacteria, viruses, and other bugs and is sometimes considered the same as decontamination.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:19
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Decontamination, however, may also include the removal of noxious toxins and could pertain to the elimination of chemicals or radiation.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:20
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: The removal of nonliving toxins, such as radiation, from a surface would, therefore, be decontamination but not disinfection.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:21
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Its useful to know the difference between a disinfectant, an antibiotic, and an antiseptic.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21:22
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: While disinfectants kill bacteria and viruses on the surface of nonliving tissue, antiseptics kill microbes on living tissue surfaces.

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_21
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Natural substances can be used in home remedies through several methods, including the following: Teas: a hot drink made by infusing the dried, crushed leaves of a plant in boiling water.

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Tinctures: plant extracts made by soaking herbs in a liquid (such as water, grain alcohol, or vinegar) for a specified length of time, then straining and discarding the plant material (also known as a decoction).

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26:13
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
text: Essential oils: liquids comprised of highly concentrated aromatic mixtures of natural compounds obtained from plants.

id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26:14
chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015

chunk_id: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015_chunk_26
source: The Ultimate Survival Medicine Guide - Emergency Preparedness for Any Disaster 2015
